newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle crew release ozone satellite.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle crew release ozone satellite.

text.p: The space shuttle Discovery soared into orbit on Thursday and set free a German-built satellite for a health check on earth's ozone layer.

The 7,000-lb (3,200-kg) spacecraft, known as CRISTA-SPAS was hauled overboard by the shuttle's robot arm at 6:27 p.m. EDT (2227 GMT) as the orbiting craft sailed 175 miles (280 km) above the earth, just south of Alaska.
"CRISTA is deployed," radioed shuttle commander Curt Brown.
The deployment was delayed about 30 minutes because of minor communications difficulties between the spacecraft and its control room at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre.
The spacecraft is equipped with two instruments for monitoring depletion of the earth's protective ozone layer and was to fly free of the shuttle for nine days before being picked up again.
Earlier on Thursday, Discovery blasted off from its Florida launch pad into a hazy summer sky at 10:41 a.m. EDT (1441 GMT) after a trouble-free countdown.
Shuttle skipper Brown was accompanied by co-pilot Kent Rominger, mission specialists Jan Davis, Robert Curbeam and Stephen Robinson and Canadian researcher Bjarni Tryggvason.
Minutes before the liftoff, controllers wished a happy birthday to Rominger, who turned 41 on Thursday.
"We're about to light your candles," orbiter test director Roger Gillette said.
"Thanks for that birthday wish," Rominger replied from the cockpit. "They'll be the two best candles I've ever had."

The rain showers and thick clouds that forecasters had feared might delay the shuttle's launch never materialised, but hazy conditions and patchy cloud obscured most of the shuttle's thundering climb to orbit.

During the 11-day flight, the crew planned to point a telescope at Comet Hale-Bopp, test a Japanese robot arm intended for use on the planned international space station, and grow colon cancer cells for medical research.
Shuttle skipper Curt Brown told a recent news conference the mission is "just jam packed full of activities. We have about everything."
Tryggvason, a Canadian scientist who was born in Reykjavik, Iceland, is flying aboard the shuttle to test a device designed to isolate delicate experiments from vibrations on the space station.
The president of Iceland, Olafur Ragnar Grimsson, watched the launch from a VIP viewing site four miles (6.5 km) from the pad.
"Splendid. The noise and vibrations were an unforgettable experience," he said. "We are a nation of discoverers and settlers and we consider this a continuation of a great Viking tradition."
Discovery is due to return to earth at the Florida spaceport on Aug. 18.
